{{Short description|Measure in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] is said to be '''saturated''' if every locally measurable set is also [[measurable]].<ref>Bogachev, Vladmir (2007). ''Measure Theory Volume 2''. Springer. {{isbn|978-3-540-34513-8}}.</ref>  A set <math>E</math>, not necessarily measurable, is said to be a '''{{visible anchor|locally measurable set}}''' if for every measurable set <math>A</math> of finite measure, <math>E \cap A</math> is measurable.  [[Σ-finite measure|<math>\sigma</math>-finite]] measures and measures arising as the restriction of [[outer measure]]s are saturated.
